subject: Ch4: Top-Down Parsing (Hard)
description: Hard-level MCQs on recursive-descent and predictive LL(1) parsing, FIRST and FOLLOW computation, LL(1) table construction and conflicts, error recovery, and grammar conditions for top-down parsing.

questions.text: For the grammar S → A a, A → α | ε with FIRST(α)={b}, FOLLOW(A) must contain:
options: ε, since A is nullable and therefore propagates the empty string into its own FOLLOW set
the end-marker $ only, as A is the rightmost symbol able to terminate the entire derivation
b, because the symbols that can begin α are always copied directly into FOLLOW(A)
a
questions.shortExplanation: A is followed by terminal a in S → A a.
questions.explanation: Because A is immediately followed by the terminal a in the production S → A a, FOLLOW(A) includes a (so the ε-alternative is chosen on lookahead a).

questions.text: An LL(1) parsing-table conflict for nonterminal A on terminal t means:
options: FIRST(A) is empty, so the parser can never predict any production for A on lookahead t
A has no productions and therefore must be removed from the grammar before building the table
t is a nonterminal that was mistakenly placed in a terminal column of the parsing table
Two distinct productions of A are both applicable on the same lookahead t, so the table cell M[A,t] holds multiple entries and the parser cannot choose deterministically
questions.shortExplanation: Multiple productions valid on the same lookahead = conflict.
questions.explanation: If more than one production for A can be predicted on lookahead t, the table cell M[A,t] holds multiple entries, so the grammar is not LL(1).

questions.text: A grammar with a production A → A α (left recursion) cannot be LL(1) because:
options: The predictive parser would have to expand A and predict the same production A → A α again before consuming any input symbol, causing unbounded infinite recursion
FIRST(A α) is empty, leaving the parser with no terminal on which to predict the production
FOLLOW(A) is undefined whenever a nonterminal appears as the first symbol of its own production
It has too many terminals for a single lookahead symbol to distinguish the alternatives
questions.shortExplanation: Left recursion makes prediction loop with no input consumed.
questions.explanation: Predicting A → Aα requires expanding A again on the same lookahead without consuming input, so a top-down predictive parser loops infinitely.

questions.text: If ε ∈ FIRST(α) for production A → α, the LL(1) table places A → α under every terminal in:
options: the whole terminal alphabet, because a nullable production may be predicted on any lookahead at all
FIRST(α) only, ignoring FOLLOW(A) entirely even though the right side can derive the empty string
FIRST(α)\{ε} together with every terminal in FOLLOW(A), because α is nullable
FOLLOW(A) only, discarding the terminals that begin α
questions.shortExplanation: Use FIRST(α) minus ε, plus FOLLOW(A) when nullable.
questions.explanation: When α can derive ε, the production is entered under FIRST(α) (excluding ε) and additionally under each terminal in FOLLOW(A).

questions.text: Two productions A → α | β satisfy the LL(1) condition only if:
options: FIRST(α) and FIRST(β) overlap on at least one terminal so the parser can share a column
FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅, and additionally, if β can derive ε (β ⇒ ε), then FIRST(α) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅ must also hold
α and β are identical right-hand sides that simply happen to be written as two separate rules
Both α and β can derive the empty string, making the nonterminal A nullable in two ways
questions.shortExplanation: Disjoint FIRSTs; the nullable one must avoid FOLLOW clashes.
questions.explanation: LL(1) requires the alternatives' FIRST sets be disjoint, and the nullable alternative's selection set (via FOLLOW) must not overlap the other's FIRST.

questions.text: For E → T E', E' → + T E' | ε, T → F T', T' → * F T', F → ( E ) | id, FIRST(E) equals:
options: { +, * }, the operators that can appear once an expression has already begun
{ id, +, * }, combining the operand start with the binary operator symbols
{ ε, ( }, since E is nullable and may also begin with a left parenthesis
questions.shortExplanation: E starts wherever F starts: ( or id.
questions.explanation: FIRST(E)=FIRST(T)=FIRST(F)={ (, id } because E ⇒ T ⇒ F and F begins with '(' or 'id'.

questions.text: In the same expression grammar, FOLLOW(E') is:
options: { id, (, ) }, the symbols that can begin or end a parenthesized factor
{ *, +, $ }, every operator together with the end-of-input marker
{ + }, the operator introduced by the recursive E' production itself
questions.shortExplanation: E' is followed by whatever follows E: ) and $.
questions.explanation: Since E → T E' and E' → + T E', E' ends an E, so FOLLOW(E') = FOLLOW(E) = { ), $ }.

questions.text: Recursive-descent WITHOUT backtracking is possible exactly when the grammar is:
options: LL(1)
Right-linear only, restricting every production to at most one trailing nonterminal symbol
Left-recursive, so each nonterminal can expand itself without first consuming any input
Ambiguous, because multiple parse trees give the parser several productions to choose from
questions.shortExplanation: Predictive (no backtrack) recursive descent ⇔ LL(1).
questions.explanation: A single lookahead chooses each production deterministically precisely when the grammar is LL(1); otherwise backtracking or more lookahead is needed.

questions.text: During table-driven predictive parsing, the action when the stack top is a terminal that matches the input is to:
options: Replace it using a production drawn from the parsing table cell for that terminal symbol
Report an error because terminals should never appear on top of the parsing stack
Pop the matched terminal off the stack and advance the input pointer to the next token
Push the FOLLOW set of the terminal so later reductions can synchronize on those tokens
questions.shortExplanation: Match terminal: pop and advance.
questions.explanation: When the top-of-stack terminal equals the current input symbol, the parser pops it and consumes the input, matching one token.

questions.text: Panic-mode recovery in predictive parsing typically uses which set to choose synchronizing tokens for nonterminal A?
options: All nonterminals, treating every grammar symbol as an equally valid synchronization point
FIRST(A) only, skipping ahead until A can begin
The empty set, since recovery deliberately ignores all FIRST and FOLLOW information
FOLLOW(A), and sometimes also FIRST(A), as synchronizing tokens for the nonterminal A
questions.shortExplanation: Synchronize on FOLLOW(A) (and FIRST(A)).
questions.explanation: Tokens in FOLLOW(A) are good synchronization points (pop A and resume); FIRST(A) tokens may be used to skip input until A can begin.

questions.text: A grammar that is left-factored and free of left recursion is:
options: Always ambiguous, because left factoring introduces overlapping alternatives in the process
Necessary but not sufficient for LL(1), since FIRST/FOLLOW conflicts may still remain
Guaranteed to be LL(1), since removing those two defects always eliminates every table conflict
Never parseable top-down once the original left recursion has been transformed away
questions.shortExplanation: Those conditions are necessary, not sufficient, for LL(1).
questions.explanation: Removing left recursion and left factoring are prerequisites, but FIRST/FOLLOW conflicts can still arise, so the grammar may still not be LL(1).

questions.text: For A → α where α does NOT derive ε, the columns in which A → α appears are exactly:
options: FIRST(α)
FOLLOW(A), the terminals that may follow A once its production has been fully reduced
FIRST(A) ∪ FOLLOW(A), combining start and following terminals
the whole alphabet, since a non-nullable production may still be predicted on any token
questions.shortExplanation: Non-nullable α ⇒ only FIRST(α) columns.
questions.explanation: If α cannot derive ε, the production is predicted only on the terminals that can begin α, i.e., FIRST(α); FOLLOW is not involved.

questions.text: Which grammar fragment causes an UNAVOIDABLE FIRST/FIRST conflict for LL(1)?
options: A → a B | c D, whose two alternatives begin with distinct terminals a and c
A → a B | a C
A → ( A ) | id, with one parenthesized alternative and one atomic identifier alternative
A → b | c, where each alternative starts with its own separate terminal symbol
questions.shortExplanation: Both alternatives start with 'a' → FIRST/FIRST clash.
questions.explanation: A → aB | aC have overlapping FIRST sets ({a}), so a single lookahead cannot choose; left factoring is required to fix it.

questions.text: The end-of-input marker $ is introduced into LL(1) parsing so that:
options: Every nonterminal becomes nullable and can therefore be popped on any lookahead token
FOLLOW(start symbol) contains $, which enables the parser to predict acceptance and apply nullable reductions exactly at the end of the input
FIRST sets become empty once the marker is appended to the right end of the input string
Left recursion is removed automatically as soon as the marker reaches the parsing stack top
questions.shortExplanation: $ ∈ FOLLOW(S) marks legitimate end of input.
questions.explanation: Appending $ lets the parser recognize the end of input; $ in FOLLOW(S) allows nullable productions and acceptance to be predicted there.

questions.text: A FIRST/FOLLOW conflict (as opposed to FIRST/FIRST) arises when, for A → α | β:
options: α can derive the empty string (α ⇒ ε) and FOLLOW(A) has a non-empty intersection with FIRST(β)
α and β are both single terminals that happen to share the same lookahead column
FIRST(α) and FIRST(β) are disjoint and neither of the two alternatives can derive the empty string
FOLLOW(A) is empty, so the nullable alternative contributes no terminals to the table at all
questions.shortExplanation: Nullable α plus FOLLOW∩FIRST(β) ≠ ∅ ⇒ conflict.
questions.explanation: When one alternative is nullable, its selection set includes FOLLOW(A); if that overlaps the other alternative's FIRST, the table cell conflicts.

questions.text: The predictive parser declares a syntax error when:
options: M[A, a] is empty for the current top-of-stack nonterminal A and the lookahead input a
A terminal on the stack is matched against an identical terminal in the remaining input
The stack still has the start symbol while more input tokens remain to be consumed
The input pointer advances past a token already matched by the stack
questions.shortExplanation: Empty table cell ⇒ no legal move ⇒ error.
questions.explanation: If the table entry for the top nonterminal and current lookahead is empty, there is no valid production to apply, signaling a syntax error.

questions.text: Computing FIRST(X₁X₂…Xₙ): you keep adding FIRST(Xᵢ) (minus ε) while the preceding symbols are all nullable, and add ε only if:
options: X₁ is a terminal, making the whole string nullable
every symbol Xᵢ for i = 1..n can derive the empty string ε
the last symbol Xₙ is a terminal that already appears inside FOLLOW of the first symbol
FOLLOW(X₁) contains ε, signalling that the leading symbol may be skipped during prediction
questions.shortExplanation: ε ∈ FIRST(string) only if all symbols are nullable.
questions.explanation: The whole concatenation is nullable exactly when every symbol can derive ε; otherwise FIRST stops at the first non-nullable symbol.

questions.text: Why does eliminating left recursion change the parse tree shape but NOT the language?
options: It rewrites the productions into an equivalent right-recursive form that still generates exactly the same set of strings, leaving the language unchanged
It makes the grammar ambiguous by allowing each string to obtain two distinct derivations
It deletes some sentences that the original left-recursive grammar was able to generate
It adds new terminals to the alphabet so the transformed grammar can express more sentences
questions.shortExplanation: Right-recursive rewrite preserves the language.
questions.explanation: The transformation produces an equivalent grammar (same language) but with right recursion, so the generated strings are unchanged though tree shapes differ.

questions.text: For T' → * F T' | ε in the expression grammar, FOLLOW(T') is:
options: { ε, +, ) }, including the empty string since T' is a nullable nonterminal
{ * }, the single operator that introduces the recursive T' production itself
{ id, (, * }, the operand starters together with the multiplication operator
questions.shortExplanation: T' is followed by what follows T: +, ), $.
questions.explanation: Since T → F T' and T' ends a T, FOLLOW(T') = FOLLOW(T) = FIRST(E') extended with FOLLOW(E) = { +, ), $ }.

questions.text: Predictive parsing is fundamentally limited compared with LR parsing because LL(1):
options: Requires ambiguous grammars in order to have more than one production per table cell
Cannot use a stack, so it must keep the entire parse state in a fixed set of registers
Produces a rightmost derivation in reverse the way shift-reduce bottom-up parsers do
Must decide the production from the top of a rule with only one lookahead, before seeing the full right side
questions.shortExplanation: LL commits early; LR decides after seeing the handle.
questions.explanation: LL(1) must choose a production from a nonterminal's left end using one lookahead, whereas LR delays the decision until a full handle is on the stack, making LR more powerful.

questions.text: If a nonterminal A has productions A → ε | a A, then on lookahead 'b' (where b ∈ FOLLOW(A)) the parser:
options: Applies A → a A, expecting the lookahead b to begin the recursive part of the production
Applies A → ε
Reports an error immediately because b does not belong to FIRST of the production a A
Pushes b onto the parsing stack and waits for a later production to consume that token
questions.shortExplanation: Lookahead in FOLLOW(A) selects the ε-production.
questions.explanation: Since 'b' is not in FIRST(aA)={a} but is in FOLLOW(A), the nullable production A → ε is predicted, popping A.

questions.text: Which is TRUE about recursive-descent parsers with backtracking?
options: They require an LR table to be built in advance before any alternative can be attempted
They are always linear time regardless of how many alternatives each nonterminal provides
They can handle some non-LL(1) grammars by trying alternatives and backing up, but in the worst case this repeated re-parsing may take exponential time
They cannot parse arithmetic expressions because operator precedence defeats backtracking
questions.shortExplanation: Backtracking widens coverage but risks exponential time.
questions.explanation: By trying alternatives and backing up, such parsers accept grammars LL(1) cannot, but repeated re-parsing can blow up to exponential time.

questions.text: The selection (predict) set of a production A → α is best described as:
options: FIRST(α), plus the terminals of FOLLOW(A) whenever the right side α is nullable
FIRST(A) only, taking the start terminals of the nonterminal rather than of this right side
The set of all terminals, since any lookahead might trigger it
FOLLOW(A) always, regardless of whether the right side α is able to derive the empty string
questions.shortExplanation: Predict set = FIRST(α) (+ FOLLOW(A) if nullable).
questions.explanation: The lookaheads on which A → α is chosen are FIRST(α), augmented by FOLLOW(A) when α can derive ε; disjoint predict sets ⇒ LL(1).

questions.text: Left factoring A → if E then S | if E then S else S produces:
options: A → E then S else S, dropping the leading keyword entirely
A → if A' ,  A' → E, factoring only the keyword while leaving the rest of the rule unshared
A → if E | then S, splitting the shared prefix across two unrelated alternatives
A → if E then S A',  A' → else S | ε, factoring out the shared 'if E then S' prefix
questions.shortExplanation: Factor the common 'if E then S' prefix; tail is optional else.
questions.explanation: The shared prefix 'if E then S' is factored out, leaving A' → else S | ε, which exposes (but does not by itself resolve) the dangling-else choice.

questions.text: A grammar can be unambiguous yet still NOT LL(1). This shows that:
options: Ambiguity is required for LL(1) parsing tables
LL(1) is a strictly stronger requirement than mere unambiguity of the grammar
LL(1) and unambiguity are equivalent properties that always hold or fail together for a grammar
All unambiguous grammars are left-recursive
questions.shortExplanation: LL(1) ⇒ unambiguous, but not conversely.
questions.explanation: Every LL(1) grammar is unambiguous, but many unambiguous grammars fail LL(1) due to FIRST/FIRST or FIRST/FOLLOW conflicts.

questions.text: In the predictive parser, when the top of stack is nonterminal A and lookahead is a, the parser:
options: Skips a token of input and leaves the nonterminal A in place for the next parsing step
Halts and accepts as soon as a nonterminal is on top
Replaces A on the stack with the right-hand side of M[A,a], pushed in reverse
Pops A and advances the input pointer as if A were a terminal
questions.shortExplanation: Expand A by the table-chosen production (RHS reversed).
questions.explanation: For a nonterminal on top, the parser consults M[A,a], replacing A with that production's right-hand side (pushed so the leftmost symbol is on top).

questions.text: Which condition makes FOLLOW relevant when building the LL(1) table?
options: Whenever a production right side is non-nullable
For every production unconditionally, since FOLLOW always supplements the FIRST-based columns
Only for nullable productions, whose right side α can derive ε
Never; only FIRST sets matter for the table
questions.shortExplanation: FOLLOW is used only for nullable right sides.
questions.explanation: FOLLOW(A) contributes table columns for A → α only when α can derive ε; otherwise FIRST(α) alone determines the columns.

questions.text: Suppose A → B C, B ⇒ ε is possible, and FIRST(C) = { d }. Then FIRST(A) includes:
options: { ε } only, treating A as purely nullable because its first symbol B can derive the empty string
FOLLOW(A), since whatever can follow A also determines what may begin its derivations
only FIRST(B)\{ε}, ignoring C even though B may vanish and let C supply the first symbol
FIRST(B)\{ε} together with the terminal d from FIRST(C), since B may vanish (and ε is included only if C is also nullable so that A itself can derive ε)
questions.shortExplanation: B nullable ⇒ add FIRST(C) too.
questions.explanation: Because B can vanish, the first symbol of A may come from C, so FIRST(A) = (FIRST(B)\{ε}) ∪ FIRST(C), with ε only if both are nullable.

questions.text: Why is LL(1) parsing called 'predictive'?
options: It guesses the input tokens before they arrive and verifies the guess against the actual stream
It predicts the target machine code that the front end will eventually have to generate
It predicts which production to apply from the lookahead before expanding the nonterminal A
It predicts the FOLLOW sets at run time instead of computing them ahead of parsing
questions.shortExplanation: It predicts the production from one lookahead.
questions.explanation: The parser uses the single lookahead token to predict (choose) the correct production deterministically, hence 'predictive' parsing.

questions.text: Converting a left-recursive expression grammar for top-down use, the new nonterminal (e.g., E') most commonly has a production ending in:
options: ε (the empty string), so the introduced nonterminal is right-recursive and terminates
left recursion again, because the transformation merely relocates the recursive call site
a terminal only, forcing every alternative of the new nonterminal to consume input first
the start symbol, so the introduced nonterminal restarts the derivation from the top
questions.shortExplanation: The tail nonterminal terminates with ε.
questions.explanation: After eliminating left recursion, the introduced nonterminal (E' → + T E' | ε) is right-recursive and bottoms out at ε, enabling predictive parsing.
